newsitem.title: UK: Broad-based banks to cope best with EMU - Citibank.
newsitem.headline: Broad-based banks to cope best with EMU - Citibank.

text.p: Banks will find it increasingly tough to stay ahead of the pack in the run-up to and after Europe's currency union unless they have a broad range of operations, a senior forex official at Citibank said.

Richard Moore, Citibank's head of foreign exchange UK in London, told Reuters in an interview that banks dealing in a wide variety of products would become the biggest players in the financial markets.

The strength such financial institutions get from their broad base would help offset potential negative impacts when European economic and monetary union kicks off in January 1999, and those in more specialised areas will lose out to them, he said.

"I think the industry in general is overstaffed and that foreign exchange companies are being forced to look at how efficient they are... Foreign exchange has too many banks competing for too few customers," Moore said.
Streamlining to make operations more efficient was also a key to survival, while 1997 should see a continuation of bank mergers to reduce the number of participants, he said.

"There seems to be a trend among key clients to deal with fewer banks but ask more of them. I suspect the forex market will become more dominated by the top 20 organisations than it is now," Moore said.

The foreign exchange industry in general has been reducing price-making capabilities, he said, adding that Citibank itself has set up a structure of one price-making centre and decentralised marketing.

Concerning fears that European currency union would lead to less business for the foreign exchange industry, Moore said EMU would not decrease forex trade volume worldwide, although it would lead to a shrinking within Europe specifically.

In addition to the dollar's rally to multi-year highs against other major currencies since the beginning of this year, European currencies have been volatile against each other, with speculation about which countries will be able to join Europe's single currency churning the market.
Once EMU is in place, however, there would be less movement in the European forex market which would lead to an outflow of trade from currencies there.

"In Europe, there are clearly going to be fewer intra-European plays depending on which countries participate in EMU. That will have varying effects, depending on what type of organisation you work for," Moore said.
"For us, as an international bank, it's a very modest effect," Moore said.

"I think if you're talking of one of the banks based in Europe where a higher percentage of their business is intra-Europe currency trades, the effect will be more marked. So that will be a negative for the industry".

Meanwhile, the urge to trade and invest will increase if anything, spurred by the deregulation of Europe's financial industries. And in the coming years, European nations will have to come up with ways of dealing with their pension liabilities, he said, adding that these countries had a "demographic time bomb".
This would mean turning more to markets outside Europe, and there have been clear signs in recent years of growing interest in foreign exchange in the emerging markets.

"One initiative would be a search for returns from outside the G10 countries. I think this will lead to a significant increase in volume outside the three major blocs -- the dollar, mark and yen," Moore said.
